title: The true person
hook: the untrue person boasts of family and learning; the true person just practices

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta's skill, and your line, one by one. Did you take one part of a mood and watch it change? Today, a test anyone can fail. Day four hundred eighty-five.

Every group has one. The person who mentions, within five minutes, where they went to school. Or how long they've been coming. Or that they read the book in the original. Sometimes it's someone else. Sometimes, honestly, it's us. The hundred and thirteenth discourse is the Buddha's portrait of exactly this, set among monks, where you'd think it couldn't happen. It's called the discourse on the true person. And the untrue person in it isn't lazy or wicked. He's often quite accomplished. Today: the true person.
screen: `WHERE THEY WENT TO SCHOOL.` → `HOW LONG THEY'VE BEEN COMING.` → `THE TRUE PERSON, AND THE UNTRUE.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is sappurisa, a good person, a true person. The Buddha builds it by contrast. Here is an untrue person, he says. He went forth from a high-ranking family. And so he praises himself and looks down on others: I'm from a noble family, these other monks aren't. Then the list goes on, and it's long. From a wealthy family. Famous. Gets plenty of robes and food. Learned. An expert in the discipline. A gifted teacher. Lives in the forest. Wears rag robes. Eats only once a day. Each time, the same move: I have this, they don't. The list even reaches the deep meditative absorptions. An untrue person can reach real stillness and then boast about that too. Now the true person. He has the same family, the same learning, the same forest hut. But he reflects: greed, hatred and delusion are not destroyed by being from a noble family. Someone from an ordinary family who practices the teaching well is worthy of honor. So he puts the practice first. He doesn't praise himself, and he doesn't look down on others. And with the absorptions, the text goes further: the true person doesn't even build an identity out of them. Whatever he imagines a state to be, it's already otherwise. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. He doesn't say good families, learning or forest life are bad. Plenty of his best students had all three. The test isn't what you have. It's what you do with it in the room: lift yourself, or just practice.
screen: `SAPPURISA: THE TRUE PERSON` · `I HAVE THIS, THEY DON'T` · `GREED ISN'T ENDED BY FAMILY` · `PUT THE PRACTICE FIRST` · then, large: `NO BOAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: practice without boasting. Sit, and let the breath be ordinary. Think of one thing you're quietly proud of: a degree, a skill, years of practice, a streak. Hold it for a moment. Then notice whether there's a little lift in it, an I have this. No need to scold it. Just set it down beside you, and come back to the breath, which doesn't care about any of it. The bell holds the time.
The true person. Sappurisa: the one who has family, learning or deep practice, and still doesn't praise himself or look down on others. Today's word.
Your line: no boast. Today, the next time you're about to mention something impressive about yourself, let the sentence go unsaid and just listen. Day four hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: In Buddhist monasteries seniority is counted by years since ordination, not by family, wealth or learning, and many teachers warn students against comparing themselves with others over meditative attainments.

match.prompt: true and untrue: tap the pairs.
pairs: praises himself, looks down on others

myth: MN 113 says good families and learning are bad
it says they don't end greed, hatred and delusion; what matters is practice and not boasting.
the untrue person in MN 113 can reach deep meditative states
the list reaches the absorptions: even real stillness can become something to boast about.
the true person, in the text, refuses to live in the forest
he may live in the forest too; he just doesn't use it to lift himself above others.

fork.setup: you're a monk from a noble family, sitting with monks who aren't. what does the true person reflect, according to MN 113?
options: my family gives me a head start.
greed and hatred aren't ended by family; practice is what counts.
I should hide where I come from.
fork.reveal: the true person sees that family doesn't destroy greed, hatred or delusion, and honors anyone who practices well.

original.note: Pali sappurisa: a good, true person. MN 113 sets it against asappurisa, the untrue person.

trapdoor: what you thought: a true person is someone very accomplished.
what it means: a true person may be accomplished, but doesn't praise himself or look down on others for it.
what a scholar hears: MN 113 runs the same contrast through birth, wealth, fame, learning, ascetic practices and even the jhanas, ending with non-identification with the highest attainments.

notes: MN 113 paraphrased; the list of grounds for boasting is condensed. Confirm the order and members (family, wealth, fame, requisites, learning, Vinaya expertise, teaching, forest dwelling, rag robes, alms food, one-session eating, jhanas).
The line 'whatever he imagines a state to be, it's already otherwise' paraphrases the sutta's 'yena yena hi mannanti, tato tam hoti annatha'; confirm the paraphrase is fair.
